title: Ability Estimation
Classification Accuracy and Consistency
text: many testing contexts, test scores used assign examinees performance categories — example, pass/fail decisions placement proficiency levels. Two indices quantify quality classification decisions: Classification Accuracy (CA): probability examinee correctly classified based true latent ability. Classification Consistency (CC): probability classification result two independent administrations test. indices essential supporting valid score interpretations high-stakes settings. data repeated test administrations rarely available, single-administration estimation procedures based IRT models commonly used. irtQ implements two IRT-based estimation methods: functions support two estimation approaches: D-method (distribution-based): integrates conditional indices population ability distribution specified quadrature points weights. approach appropriate empirical ability distribution (e.g., posterior quadrature weights IRT calibration) available. P-method (person-based): averages conditional indices individual ability estimates sample examinees. functions return list five elements: $confusion: confusion matrix (rows = true level, columns = expected level), $marginal: data frame marginal CA CC indices per performance level plus overall marginal row, $conditional: data frame conditional CA CC theta (node), $prob.level: data frame probability assigned level theta (node), $cutscore: cut scores used analysis (observed score scale).

title: DIF Detection
text: simulate 40-item dichotomous test (3PLM) 1,000 examinees per group. DIF introduced six items: Items 1–2: Uniform DIF — focal group higher difficulty parameter (b+0.5b + 0.5) discrimination parameter unchanged. Items 3–4: Nonuniform DIF — focal group lower discrimination parameter (×0.5a \times 0.5) difficulty parameter unchanged. Items 5–6: Mixed DIF — focal group lower discrimination parameter (×0.5a \times 0.5) higher difficulty parameter (b+0.5b + 0.5), making items less discriminating harder focal group. Items 7–40: DIF. focal group slightly lower mean ability (μ=−0.3\mu = -0.3) reference group (μ=0\mu = 0), representing realistic impact condition. Next, calibrate item parameters using pooled data estimate ability scores. RDIF framework requires ability estimates based pooled (aggregate) item parameters, calibration scoring must performed combined data regardless group membership (Lim et al. 2022).
code: J   <- 40     # number of items N_R <- 1000   # reference group size N_F <- 1000   # focal group size  # Base item parameters (no DIF) shared by both groups set.seed(100) a_base <- round(runif(J, 0.7, 1.7), 2) b_base <- round(runif(J, -4.0, 4.0), 2) g_base <- rep(0.15, J)  # Reference group item metadata (no DIF) meta_ref <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(a = a_base, b = b_base, g = g_base),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Focal group item metadata: DIF injected into items 1–6 a_focal      <- a_base b_focal      <- b_base b_focal[1:2] <- b_base[1:2] + 0.5          # uniform DIF: harder for focal a_focal[3:4] <- a_base[3:4] * 0.5          # nonuniform DIF: less discriminating a_focal[5:6] <- a_base[5:6] * 0.5          # mixed DIF: less discriminating ... b_focal[5:6] <- b_base[5:6] + 0.5          # ... and harder for focal  meta_foc <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(a = a_focal, b = b_focal, g = g_base),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Simulate ability parameters: reference N(0,1), focal N(-0.3,1) theta_R <- rnorm(N_R, mean =  0.0, sd = 1) theta_F <- rnorm(N_F, mean = -0.3, sd = 1)  # Simulate item responses separately for each group resp_R <- simdat(x = meta_ref, theta = theta_R, D = 1.702) resp_F <- simdat(x = meta_foc, theta = theta_F, D = 1.702)  # Pool responses and define group membership vector (0 = reference, 1 = focal) resp_pool <- rbind(resp_R, resp_F) group_vec <- c(rep(0, N_R), rep(1, N_F))  cat("Pooled data:", nrow(resp_pool), "examinees x", ncol(resp_pool), "items\n") #> Pooled data: 2000 examinees x 40 items # Calibrate item parameters from the pooled data mod_pool <- est_irt(   data       = resp_pool,   D          = 1.702,   model      = "3PLM",   cats       = 2,   use.gprior = TRUE,   gprior     = list(dist = "beta", params = c(4, 16)),   EmpHist    = TRUE,   verbose    = FALSE )  meta_pool <- mod_pool$par.est  # Estimate ability using ML method # ML is recommended for RDIF analysis as it provides point estimates # unaffected by prior distribution assumptions [@lim_etal2022] score_pool <- est_score(   x      = meta_pool,   data   = resp_pool,   D      = 1.702,   method = "ML",   range  = c(-5, 5) )$est.theta

Classical Test Theory (CTT) summarizes examinees total (proportion) correct score items observed difficulty (p-value) point-biserial correlation. straightforward, CTT well-known limitations: Sample dependence: item statistics (difficulty, discrimination) change examinee group, person scores change item set item-level probability model: CTT tell us probability specific person answers specific item correctly Limited equating: comparing scores across different test forms requires strong assumptions Item Response Theory (IRT) addresses limitations modeling probability response function latent trait θ\theta (ability, proficiency, attitude) item parameters. Key advantages : Invariance: item parameters depend ability distribution calibration sample; person parameters depend particular items administered Item-level modeling: item characteristic curve describing response probability changes θ\theta Common scale: items persons placed θ\theta continuum, enabling equating, adaptive testing, longitudinal measurement

Example (4-category GRM item, K=4K = 4): b1=−1.5b_1 = -1.5: Examinees θ≈−1.5\theta \approx -1.5 50% chance scoring 1 higher b2=0.0b_2 = 0.0: Examinees θ≈0\theta \approx 0 50% chance scoring 2 higher b3=1.2b_3 = 1.2: Examinees θ≈1.2\theta \approx 1.2 50% chance scoring 3 (top category)

Parameters: aa: single discrimination parameter item b1,b2,…,bK−1b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{K-1}: step parameters (also called threshold parameters), bvb_v governs transition category v−1v-1 category vv. Unlike GRM thresholds, GPCM step parameters need ordered. title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: est_irt() function implements Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation via Expectation-Maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). avoid incidental parameter problem (estimating individual ability θ\theta leads inconsistent item parameter estimates sample size grows), algorithm treats θ\theta random variable following specific prior distribution, typically g(θ)∼N(0,1)g(\theta) \sim N(0, 1). Note Item Types: clarity simplicity, mathematical formulation explanations presented using dichotomous (binary) items, although underlying logic seamlessly extends polytomous item response models. integrating latent variable θ\theta joint likelihood, obtain marginal log-likelihood observed data, item parameters (𝚫\boldsymbol{\Delta}) parameters estimated: log⁡L(𝚫∣𝐔)=∑=1Nlog⁡∫−∞∞L(𝐮i∣θ)g(θ)dθ \log L(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mid \mathbf{U}) = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta)\, g(\theta) d\theta L(𝐮i∣θ)L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta) likelihood observing examinee ii’s response pattern 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_i given ability θ\theta, g(θ)g(\theta) prior density function latent ability. Using KK-point quadrature, continuous integral approximated discrete summation KK quadrature points θk\theta_k prior weights wkw_k (weights standard normal distribution): log⁡Lmarginal(𝚫∣𝐔)≈∑=1Nlog⁡∑k=1KL(𝐮i∣θk)wk \log L_{marginal}(\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mid \mathbf{U}) \approx \sum_{=1}^{N} \log \sum_{k=1}^{K} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_k)\, w_k maximize marginal log-likelihood, analytically intractable due summation inside logarithm, est_irt() iteratively executes following E-step M-step convergence: E-step (Expectation): Computing Artificial Sufficient Statistics examinee response pattern 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_i, algorithm first computes posterior probability θ\theta quadrature point θk\theta_k: P(θk∣𝐮i)=L(𝐮i∣θk)wk∑m=1KL(𝐮i∣θm)wm P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) = \frac{L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_k)\, w_k}{\sum_{m=1}^{K} L(\mathbf{u}_i \mid \theta_m)\, w_m} Using individual posteriors, algorithm aggregates data across NN examinees construct artificial sufficient statistics quadrature point: Expected number examinees (nkn_k) θk\theta_k: nk=∑=1NP(θk∣𝐮i) n_k = \sum_{=1}^{N} P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) Expected number correct responses (rjkr_{jk}) item jj θk\theta_k: rjk=∑=1NuijP(θk∣𝐮i) r_{jk} = \sum_{=1}^{N} u_{ij} P(\theta_k \mid \mathbf{u}_i) M-step (Maximization): Item--Item Parameter Optimization M-step, algorithm treats nkn_k rjkr_{jk} fixed constants. decoupling joint likelihood, parameters item jj can updated independently (item--item) maximizing expected complete-data log-likelihood (QQ-function): ℓj(𝛅j)=∑k=1K[rjklnPj(θk)+(nk−rjk)ln(1−Pj(θk))] \ell_j(\boldsymbol{\delta}_j) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left[ r_{jk} \ln P_j(\theta_k) + (n_k - r_{jk}) \ln (1 - P_j(\theta_k)) \right] 𝛅j\boldsymbol{\delta}_j denotes item parameter vector (e.g., slope aja_j difficulty bjb_j 2PL model) Pj(θk)P_j(\theta_k) item response function. est_irt() numerically optimizes function item using Newton-Raphson root-finding techniques. Extension Polytomous Items: formulation uses dichotomous items ease illustration, underlying MMLE-EM framework generalizes polytomous item response models (e.g., Graded Response Model, Generalized Partial Credit Model). polytomous items, expected complete-data log-likelihood incorporates multinomial category response probabilities Pjv(θk)P_{jv}(\theta_k) corresponding expected category frequencies rjvkr_{jvk} category vv, maintaining identical decoupling optimization structure. Convergence two-step cycle (E M) repeats. algorithm terminates maximum absolute change item parameter estimates consecutive iterations smaller convergence threshold specified Etol argument. Key advantages MMLE-EM: require individual ability estimates (θ\theta “integrated ”) Handles missing data naturally Allows prior distributions item parameters numerical stability

text: 1-parameter logistic model (1PLM), also known Rasch model, simplest IRT model dichotomous items. assumes: items equal discrimination (slopes) Items differ difficulty (location) guessing (lower asymptote = 0) Mathematical form: P(Y=1∣θ)=11+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)) P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))} aa constrained equal across items (fixed 1). text: EmpHist = TRUE ? Instead assuming θ ~ N(μ, σ²), EM algorithm estimates empirical density quadrature point using Woods (2007) method. mean variance still constrained group.mean group.var scale identification, shape distribution estimated freely data. use EmpHist = TRUE: ✅ Sample size sufficiently large ✅ suspect ability distribution non-normal (e.g., bimodal, skewed) ✅ want avoid strong distributional assumptions `  Interpretation: close match normal curve suggests normality assumption reasonable; EmpHist = FALSE sufficient. Notable deviations (e.g., skewness, multimodality) suggest empirical histogram captures real population structure EmpHist = TRUE preferred. example, data generated N(0, 1), empirical estimate closely follows normal overlay.
code: # Estimate with empirical histogram mod_bin_emp <- est_irt(   data       = resp_bin,   D          = 1.702,   model      = "2PLM",   cats       = 2,   item.id    = paste0("ITEM", 1:25),   EmpHist    = TRUE,     # ← Estimate empirical distribution   group.mean = 0,        # ← Mean constrained to 0 for identification   group.var  = 1,        # ← Variance constrained to 1 for identification   Etol       = 0.001,   MaxE       = 200,   se         = TRUE,   verbose    = FALSE )  # Extract the estimated empirical distribution emp_hist <- mod_bin_emp$weights  # Compare empirical estimate with the N(0,1) reference curve theta_seq  <- emp_hist$theta norm_dens  <- dnorm(theta_seq, mean = 0, sd = 1) norm_dens  <- norm_dens / sum(norm_dens)   # Rescale to match histogram units  plot(emp_hist$theta, emp_hist$weight,      type = "h", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",      xlab = expression(theta),      ylab = "Density",      main = "Empirical Ability Distribution vs. Normal Prior",      ylim = c(0, max(emp_hist$weight) * 1.2)) lines(theta_seq, norm_dens, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) legend("topright",        legend = c("Empirical Histogram", "Normal(0,1)"),        col = c("steelblue", "red"),        lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(3, 2))

what: Example 4: 3PLM Calibration — Priors and Guessing Parameter Options
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: 3-parameter logistic model (3PLM) adds lower-asymptote (guessing) parameter gg 2PLM: P(Y=1∣θ)=g+(1−g)1+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)) P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) = g + \frac{(1 - g)}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))} g∈[0,1)g \[0, 1) pseudo-guessing parameter, probability correct response even low ability levels. gg can poorly identified small samples (sometimes even large samples), two primary options handling gg est_irt(): Estimate gg Beta prior (use.gprior = TRUE) — regularizes gg toward plausible range (e.g., 1/K1/K KK-option MC item), Fix gg constant value (fix.g = TRUE, g.val = ...) — appropriate number response options known guessing assumed uniform. addition, priors discrimination (aa) difficulty (bb) can applied via use.aprior use.bprior. especially useful : item discrimination estimates may unstable Items extreme difficulty values (|b|>3|b| > 3) pull bb toward unreasonable values want incorporate substantive prior knowledge (e.g., discriminations typically follow log-normal distribution certain parameters)

text: Interpretation: Strategy (use.gprior = TRUE): Beta prior gg prevents implausibly large guessing estimates allowing item-level variation gg. recommended default 5-option multiple-choice tests. Practical guideline: multiple-choice tests, start use.gprior = TRUE appropriate Beta prior. Add use.aprior use.bprior estimates unstable extreme. previous_headings: Part 3: Pretest Calibration — FAPC with est_item()
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: FAPC (Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration) treats examinee ability estimates known (fixed) constants estimates item parameters maximizing item-level likelihood conditional fixed abilities. approach widely used pretest item calibration, particularly stable group examinees already taken operational test (e.g., within CAT environment) proficiency estimates readily available. instance, CAT system, examinee encounters personalized sequence items: Operational items (scored): Used estimate update examinees’ abilities (θ\theta). Pretest items (interspersed unscored): Embedded within test accumulate response data; parameters unknown need calibrated. FAPC leverages individual θ̂\hat{\theta} values obtained operational items calibrate pretest item independently. Compared FIPC, FAPC computationally much simpler. eliminates need EM iterations, item’s parameters can estimated single, straightforward optimization process. Consequently, calibration can begin immediately soon sufficient number responses accumulate specific pretest item.

previous_headings: Part 3: Pretest Calibration — FAPC with est_item()
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: Given response uiju_{ij} examinee ii pretest item jj fixed ability estimate θ̂\hat{\theta}_i, item-level log-likelihood defined : ℓ(aj,bj)=∑=1Nlog⁡P(uij∣θ̂,aj,bj) \ell(a_j, b_j) = \sum_{=1}^{N} \log P(u_{ij} \mid \hat{\theta}_i,\, a_j,\, b_j) item parameters estimated directly maximizing log-likelihood expression via numerical optimization (e.g., using nlminb()). Unlike standard marginal maximum likelihood (MML) estimation FIPC, EM cycle involved θ\theta values treated fixed, observed data rather latent distribution integrated . Important Limitation: FAPC inherently treats estimated abilities θ̂\hat{\theta}_i true, error-free parameters (θi\theta_i), thereby ignoring ability estimation error (measurement error). omission can lead slight downward bias item discrimination estimates (aa-parameters), especially operational test relatively short θ̂\hat{\theta} estimates less precise. Additionally, prevent selection bias confounding calibration, random (non-adaptive) pretest administration design strongly preferred adaptive administration pretest items.

what: Key Advantages and Limitations of FAPC
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: ✅ Simple: Direct MLE conditional θ̂\hat{\theta}, requiring complex latent distribution assumptions. ✅ Fast: EM iterations needed, making computationally trivial. ✅ Scalable: item calibrated independently; ideal large-scale item pools real-time distributed computing. ✅ Flexible: Compatible ability estimation method (MLE, EAP, MAP) derived operational test. ⚠️ Assumes θ\theta known without error: Treating θ̂\hat{\theta} fixed constant ignores measurement error. measurement error propagates calibration, causing slight downward bias (attenuation) item discrimination estimates, especially operational form short. ⚠️ population distribution estimation: Unlike FIPC, FAPC estimate recover group-level latent trait distribution (μθ,σθ\mu_{\theta}, \sigma_{\theta}) abilities treated fixed data rather random effect.

previous_headings: Part 4: Multiple-Group Calibration with est_mg()
title: Item Parameter Estimation
text: many testing programs, different groups examinees take different test forms share common (anchor) items. Common scenarios include: Vertical scaling: Grades 3, 4, 5 take different form; common items link adjacent grades onto single developmental scale. Test form equating: Two alternate forms (Form Form B) share anchor items; goal place forms common score scale. International assessments: Different countries take translated/adapted forms; common items enable cross-national comparisons. Longitudinal studies: Different cohorts take evolving forms time; common items maintain scale continuity. Challenge: group may different ability distribution (e.g., Grade 3 examinees systematically less able Grade 5 examinees), simply pooling data across groups calibrating together confound item difficulty group ability. Solution: est_mg() simultaneously: Estimates item parameters Constrains anchor item parameters identical across groups Estimates group-specific ability distributions Places everything common scale

Group ability distributions freely estimated account population heterogeneity, unless one group fixed reference. example, consider three groups sharing items follows: est_mg() automatically constrains parameters C1 items identical across Groups 1 2, C2 items identical across Groups 2 3. chain statistical constraints links three groups onto single, unified scale.

Instead conditioning θ̂\hat{\theta}, SS-X2X^2 conditions observed summed score Xs=∑iuiX_s = \sum_{} u_i. Within summed-score group ss, expected proportion correct responses P̂(Xi=1∣Xs=s)\hat{P}(X_i = 1 \mid X_s = s) computed using Lord–Wingersky recursive algorithm (Lord & Wingersky, 1984), integrates IRF latent ability distribution without requiring individual θ̂\hat{\theta} estimates. Note. formula presented dichotomous items (scored 0/1). Kang & Chen (2008) extended SS-X2X^2 polytomous items; see Extension polytomous items paragraph . S-X2=∑sNs(x‾s−P̂s)2P̂s(1−P̂s)S\text{-}X^2 = \sum_{s} \frac{N_s \left(\bar{x}_s - \hat{P}_s\right)^2}{\hat{P}_s(1-\hat{P}_s)} NsN_s number examinees summed score ss, x‾s\bar{x}_s observed proportion correct item ii among examinees, P̂s\hat{P}_s model-based expected proportion. text: irtQ provides run_mst() carry exactly kind simulation. Given item bank, route_map, module matrix, vector true abilities (pre-generated response matrix), run_mst() simulates full MST administration every examinee — stage--stage routing final scoring — returns resulting ability estimates together module pathway examinee traveled. examples use simMST 1-3-3 panel introduced : routing module Stage 1, followed three modules varying difficulty Stages 2 3. run_mst() supports three routing strategies. Two require fixed cut scores : default, route_method = "bmat", routes examinee reachable module whose mean item difficulty closest current ability estimate, route_method = "mfi" routes reachable module highest test information function (TIF) value current estimate. third, cut-score routing (route_method = NULL), compares current estimate fixed set cut scores. Start default, bmat: closely related alternative maximum Fisher information (MFI) routing (route_method = "mfi"): instead comparing mean item difficulty, routes examinee reachable module provides highest TIF value current ability estimate. MFI routing assumes module’s TIF curve behaves intended — peaking higher harder modules theta increases, higher easier modules theta decreases. practice assumption can fail: harder module’s TIF curve may unexpectedly peak low theta value, low-ability examinees routed easy module instead get routed harder one. called anomalous routing, path reversal, opposite MST designed . Alternatively, setting route_method = NULL switches traditional cut-score routing — design commonly used operational MST programs — examinee’s intermediate ability estimate compared fixed set cut scores decide next module:

Generating response matrix simdat() feeding response argument removes source noise — also run_mst() used real, already-observed response data: five calls return kind result regardless routing rule input format used: final ability estimate (est.theta), standard error (se.theta), module pathway taken examinee (path).
code: # Generate one response matrix from a fresh set of true abilities set.seed(123) theta_true2 <- rnorm(500, mean = 0, sd = 1) resp_matrix <- simdat(x = x, theta = theta_true2, D = 1.702) # resp_matrix is an N x J matrix (N examinees x J total items in the bank)  # bmat routing on the pre-generated responses result_A <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = theta_true2,    # kept only for RMSE evaluation below   response     = resp_matrix,    # pre-generated N x J response matrix   D            = 1.702,   route_method = "bmat",   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE )  # find_cut()-based cut-score routing on the SAME responses result_B <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = theta_true2,   response     = resp_matrix,    # identical responses -> fair comparison   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_result$cut_score,   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE )  # Any RMSE difference now reflects the routing rule alone, not response noise rmse_A <- sqrt(mean((result_A$est.theta - theta_true2)^2)) rmse_B <- sqrt(mean((result_B$est.theta - theta_true2)^2)) cat(sprintf("RMSE (bmat):                 %.4f\n", rmse_A)) #> RMSE (bmat):                 0.3706 cat(sprintf("RMSE (find_cut cut scores):  %.4f\n", rmse_B)) #> RMSE (find_cut cut scores):  0.3432

what: The Challenge of Evaluating MST Panels
title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: deploying MST panel operationally, test developers need evaluate measurement quality: accurately precisely panel estimate examinee ability level latent trait θ\theta? two key evaluation metrics : Conditional Bias: average difference ability estimate θ̂\hat{\theta} true ability θ\theta, evaluated θ\theta level. Ideally, bias near zero across full ability range. Conditional Standard Error Measurement (CSEM): standard deviation ability estimates θ\theta level. Lower CSEM means precise measurement.

what: The Traditional Approach: Monte Carlo Simulation
title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: Conditional evaluation via simulation means repeating run_mst() procedure shown systematically across fixed grid ability levels, many replications grid point: Fix set true ability levels θ1,θ2,…\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots θk\theta_k, generate thousands simulated response patterns Route simulated examinee panel — exactly run_mst() — using chosen routing rule (cut scores, b-matching, maximum information) Estimate ability simulated response compute mean variance estimates Bias = mean(θ̂\hat\theta) − θk\theta_k, CSEM = Var(θ̂)\sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat\theta)} run_mst() already automates Steps 2–4 single θk\theta_k single batch replications; full evaluation just wraps loop ability grid sufficiently large number replications per grid point (Example 6 demonstrates exactly ). approach conceptually simple, looping run_mst() way inherits several practical drawbacks: Computationally inefficient: Thousands response patterns must generated scored Stochastic: Results fluctuate across simulation replications Time-consuming: Evaluating many panel designs cut score configurations requires many separate simulation runs

title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: Lim et al. (2021) proposed fundamentally different approach: instead simulating individual examinees, method directly computes exact probability distribution every possible observed score every stage pathway using recursive algorithm. key insight conditional distribution observed sum score along pathway can built stage stage using Lord–Wingersky recursion (Lord & Wingersky, 1984). Given conditional score distribution modules visited far, joint distribution next stage can computed exactly — without random sampling. core logic recursion: Stage 1: Compute P(X1=x∣θ)P(X_1 = x \mid \theta) routing module using Lord–Wingersky recursion, X1X_1 total score Stage 1. Routing: possible score xx Stage 1, determine Stage 2 module test taker routed (using cut scores). converts score distribution pathway probability. Stage 2: Stage 2 pathway, compute joint distribution P(X1+X2=s∣θ,path)P(X_1 + X_2 = s \mid \theta, \text{path}) convolving Stage 1 score distribution conditional distribution assigned Stage 2 module. Continue recursively stages. Ability estimation: Convert possible final sum score θ̂\hat\theta estimate using inverse Test Characteristic Curve (TCC) method — method implied IRT-based summed scoring. Note linear interpolation (intpol): items non-zero guessing parameters (e.g., 3PLM), minimum achievable expected sum score exceeds zero — meaning valid θ̂\hat\theta exists low observed scores (sum guessing parameters). intpol = TRUE (default), inverse TCC method applies linear interpolation point (θmin,0)(\theta_{\min},\, 0) lowest TCC-reachable score point, every possible sum score receives valid ability estimate rather NA. Evaluate: Compute conditional mean variance θ̂\hat\theta given true θ\theta, derive conditional bias CSEM. method : Exact: probability distributions computed analytically, approximated random sampling Fast: Computation takes seconds, minutes hours Deterministic: Results reproducible without simulation noise Comprehensive: panel design, cut score configuration, ability grid can evaluated single function call reval_mst() function irtQ implements recursion-based method, computing conditional bias CSEM Monte Carlo loop estimates simulation — analytically, single function call without simulation noise.

code: eval_tb <- eval_result$eval.tb  # Side-by-side plots: bias (left) and CSEM (right) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))  # Bias plot plot(   eval_tb$theta, eval_tb$bias,   type = "b", pch = 16, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,   xlab = expression(theta),   ylab = "Conditional Bias",   main = "Conditional Bias",   ylim = c(-0.3, 0.3) ) abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5) grid()  # CSEM plot plot(   eval_tb$theta, eval_tb$csem,   type = "b", pch = 16, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2,   xlab = expression(theta),   ylab = "CSEM",   main = "Conditional SEM (CSEM)",   ylim = c(0, max(eval_tb$csem) * 1.2) ) abline(h = mean(eval_tb$csem), col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5) legend("topright", legend = "Mean CSEM", lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 1.5) grid() par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) library(ggplot2) library(tidyr) library(dplyr)  eval_tb %>%   dplyr::select(theta, bias, csem) %>%   tidyr::pivot_longer(     cols      = c(bias, csem),     names_to  = "criterion",     values_to = "value"   ) %>%   ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = theta, y = value)) +   ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +   ggplot2::geom_line(aes(colour = criterion, linetype = criterion), linewidth = 1.2) +   ggplot2::geom_point(aes(shape = criterion), size = 2.5) +   ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(bias = "steelblue", csem = "darkorange")) +   ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c(bias = "solid", csem = "dashed")) +   ggplot2::labs(     x       = expression(theta),     y       = NULL,     title   = "1-3-3 MST Panel: Conditional Bias and CSEM",     colour  = NULL,     linetype = NULL,     shape   = NULL   ) +   ggplot2::theme_bw() +   ggplot2::theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))

code: # Retrieve item metadata for the easiest and hardest complete pathways # (pathway 1 = low ability; last pathway = high ability) n_paths <- nrow(eval_result$panel.info$pathway)  meta_low  <- eval_result$item.by.path$stage.3$path.1          # low-ability path meta_high <- eval_result$item.by.path[[3]][[n_paths]]          # high-ability path  theta_grid <- seq(-4, 4, 0.1)  tif_low  <- info(x = meta_low,  theta = theta_grid, D = 1.702)$tif tif_high <- info(x = meta_high, theta = theta_grid, D = 1.702)$tif  par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1)) plot(   theta_grid, tif_low,   type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,   xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Test Information",   main = "Test Information: Low-Ability vs. High-Ability Pathway",   ylim = c(0, max(c(tif_low, tif_high)) * 1.1) ) lines(theta_grid, tif_high, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend(   "topright",   legend  = c("Low-ability pathway (path 1)", "High-ability pathway (last path)"),   col     = c("steelblue", "darkorange"),   lty     = c(1, 2), lwd = 2 ) grid()

text: 1-2-2 MST panel design. Stage 1, examinees begin module 1M. Stage 1, routed either 2E (easy) 2H (hard). Stage 2, can routed either 3E 3H regardless Stage 2 module took. Routing: Stage 1 → Stage 2: θ̂<0\hat\theta < 0 → M2 (Easy), θ̂≥0\hat\theta \geq 0 → M3 (Hard) Stage 2 → Stage 3: θ̂<0\hat\theta < 0 → M4 (Easy), θ̂≥0\hat\theta \geq 0 → M5 (Hard) gives 4 pathways: M1-M2-M4, M1-M2-M5, M1-M3-M4, M1-M3-M5.

code: # 6 items per module × 5 modules = 30 items total n_per_mod <- 6  # Helper: create item metadata for one module make_mod_items <- function(a_mean, b_vec, g_val, id_prefix) {   shape_df(     par.drm  = list(       a = rep(a_mean, n_per_mod),       b = b_vec,       g = rep(g_val, n_per_mod)     ),     item.id  = paste0(id_prefix, 1:n_per_mod),     cats     = 2,     model    = "3PLM"   ) }  # Module 1 (Routing, Stage 1): moderate difficulty items_m1 <- make_mod_items(   a_mean   = 1.2,   b_vec    = c(-0.5, -0.2,  0.0,  0.2,  0.4,  0.6),   g_val    = 0.15,   id_prefix = "M1_I" )  # Module 2 (Easy, Stage 2): lower difficulty items_m2 <- make_mod_items(   a_mean   = 1.1,   b_vec    = c(-2.0, -1.6, -1.3, -1.0, -0.7, -0.4),   g_val    = 0.15,   id_prefix = "M2_I" )  # Module 3 (Hard, Stage 2): higher difficulty items_m3 <- make_mod_items(   a_mean   = 1.3,   b_vec    = c( 0.4,  0.6,  0.9,  1.2,  1.5,  1.8),   g_val    = 0.15,   id_prefix = "M3_I" )  # Module 4 (Easy, Stage 3): lowest difficulty items_m4 <- make_mod_items(   a_mean   = 1.0,   b_vec    = c(-2.5, -2.2, -1.9, -1.6, -1.3, -1.0),   g_val    = 0.15,   id_prefix = "M4_I" )  # what: Example 5: Comparing Two Cut Score Configurations
title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: Cut score placement directly affects measurement bias. Placing cuts close centre can cause mid-ability examinees routed sub-optimally. compare original c(-0.5, 0.5) cut scores wider configuration c(-1.0, 1.0) 1-3-3 panel. CSEM comparison: original vs. wider cut scores 1-3-3 panel. Wide cuts concentrate test takers middle module Stage 2 3 ability levels, tends reduce bias near centre may increase CSEM ability extremes.
code: # Alternative cut scores: wider routing bands cut_score_wide <- list(c(-1.0, 1.0), c(-1.0, 1.0))  eval_wide <- reval_mst(   x         = x,   D         = 1.702,   route_map = route_map,   module    = module,   cut_score = cut_score_wide,   theta     = theta,   range.tcc = c(-5, 5) ) tb_orig <- eval_result$eval.tb tb_wide <- eval_wide$eval.tb  par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))  # Bias comparison ylim_bias <- range(c(tb_orig$bias, tb_wide$bias, -0.4, 0.4)) plot(   tb_orig$theta, tb_orig$bias,   type = "b", pch = 16, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,   xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Conditional Bias",   main = "Bias Comparison", ylim = ylim_bias ) lines(tb_wide$theta, tb_wide$bias,       type = "b", pch = 17, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2) abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 3) legend("topright",        legend = c("Original cuts (±0.5)", "Wider cuts (±1.0)"),        col    = c("steelblue", "darkorange"),        pch    = c(16, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, cex = 0.85) grid()  # CSEM comparison ylim_csem <- c(0, max(c(tb_orig$csem, tb_wide$csem)) * 1.2) plot(   tb_orig$theta, tb_orig$csem,   type = "b", pch = 16, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,   xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "CSEM",   main = "CSEM Comparison", ylim = ylim_csem ) lines(tb_wide$theta, tb_wide$csem,       type = "b", pch = 17, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend("topright",        legend = c("Original cuts (±0.5)", "Wider cuts (±1.0)"),        col    = c("steelblue", "darkorange"),        pch    = c(16, 17), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, cex = 0.85) grid() par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

what: Example 6: Validating reval_mst() Against a run_mst() Monte Carlo Simulation
title: MST Panel Evaluation and Simulation
text: “Simulate MST Panel Performance?” section introduced run_mst() noted turning single simulation run full panel evaluation means looping θ\theta grid many replications per point — traditional Monte Carlo approach. Lim et al. (2021) validated recursion-based analytical method exactly kind simulation, closeness agreement found depended scoring method used. simulation used scoring recursion assumes throughout — equated-number-correct (ENC) score, deterministic score--θ\theta transformation conceptually analogous reval_mst()’s internal inverse-TCC scoring — simulated analytical results matched closely every θ\theta, converged replications increased. simulation instead used combination common practice — EAP routing, maximum likelihood (MLE) final score — two methods still agreed closely central ability range, diverged toward extremes, item pool carries little information MLE behaves quite differently inverse-TCC-based recursion. region close central agreement widens test length increases. reproduce second condition directly simMST panel, using scoring combination Lim et al. (2021) used validation: route_score = "EAP" routing interim stage, final_score = "ML" reported final score. Neither method matches reval_mst()’s internal inverse-TCC logic, two results expected coincide everywhere; comparison reproduce central-agreement--tail-divergence pattern Lim et al. (2021) reported. exact values stored simMST$theta needed comparison, define explicit evaluation grid Monte Carlo simulation analytical computation guaranteed line point--point: Step 1 — Monte Carlo simulation run_mst(). n_reps replications every grid point simulated single call passing full true_theta vector. Routing uses panel’s fixed cut scores (matching routing rule reval_mst() assumes), EAP routing scores ML final scores — scoring combination Lim et al. (2021) used Monte Carlo validation: Step 2 — Analytical computation reval_mst() theta_grid, comparison point--point: Step 3 — Overlay two results: Empirical bias RMSE run_mst() Monte Carlo simulation (points) overlaid analytical reval_mst() curve (line). central ability range — Lim et al. (2021) reported roughly −1.5≤θ≤1.5-1.5 \le \theta \le 1.5 scoring combination, widening longer tests — Monte Carlo points track analytical curve closely, small remaining deviations attributable sampling error n_reps = 300 replications per grid point (shrink n_reps increases). Toward extremes, two expected diverge: EAP routing ML final scoring depart reval_mst()’s internal inverse-TCC logic, departure grows item pool carries little information EAP/MLE estimates behave quite differently inverse-TCC-based recursion. mirrors pattern Lim et al. (2021) reported identical EAP-routing/MLE-final condition. Matching recursion’s scoring exactly — route_score = "INV.TCC" final_score = "INV.TCC" instead "EAP"/"ML" — close gap. reval_mst() therefore best read predicting performance panel routed scored via inverse-TCC; whenever program uses different scoring approach operationally, run_mst() simulation like one remains direct check, particularly ability levels far panel’s region peak information. Step 4 — Confirm gap closes matched scoring. final check, re-run simulation route_score = "INV.TCC" final_score = "INV.TCC", matching reval_mst()’s internal logic exactly: Comparing three tail grid points, EAP/ML condition diverged analytical curve: comparison, overlaid across full ability range: Empirical bias RMSE INV.TCC/INV.TCC run_mst() Monte Carlo simulation (points) overlaid analytical reval_mst() curve (line). table plot confirm conclusion: INV.TCC/INV.TCC condition tracks analytical bias RMSE closely across entire ability range, including extremes EAP/ML condition diverged.
code: # An explicit, independent evaluation grid theta_grid <- seq(-5, 5, 0.5) n_reps     <- 300   # simulated examinees per grid point  # Repeat each grid point n_reps times into one long vector of true abilities set.seed(2026) true_theta <- rep(theta_grid, each = n_reps) sim_mc <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = true_theta,   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_score,   route_score  = list(method = "EAP", norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41),   final_score  = list(method = "ML", range = c(-4, 4)),   se           = FALSE,   verbose      = FALSE )  # Empirical bias and RMSE at each grid point mc_tb <- data.frame(theta = true_theta, est.theta = sim_mc$est.theta) diff_mc  <- mc_tb$est.theta - mc_tb$theta bias_mc  <- tapply(diff_mc, mc_tb$theta, mean) rmse_mc  <- tapply(diff_mc, mc_tb$theta, function(d) sqrt(mean(d^2)))  mc_result <- data.frame(   theta = as.numeric(names(bias_mc)),   bias  = as.numeric(bias_mc),   rmse  = as.numeric(rmse_mc) ) mc_result <- mc_result[order(mc_result$theta), ] eval_grid <- reval_mst(   x         = x,   D         = 1.702,   route_map = route_map,   module    = module,   cut_score = cut_score,   theta     = theta_grid,   range.tcc = c(-5, 5) )  tb_grid      <- eval_grid$eval.tb tb_grid$rmse <- sqrt(tb_grid$sigma2 + tb_grid$bias^2) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))  # Bias: Monte Carlo (points) vs. analytical (line) plot(   tb_grid$theta, tb_grid$bias,   type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",   xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "Bias", main = "Bias: Simulation vs. Analytical",   ylim = range(c(tb_grid$bias, mc_result$bias, -0.3, 0.3)) ) points(mc_result$theta, mc_result$bias, pch = 16, col = "darkorange") abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 3) legend("topright",        legend = c("reval_mst() (analytical)", "run_mst() (Monte Carlo)"),        col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"), lty = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 16),        lwd = c(2, NA), cex = 0.8) grid()  # RMSE: Monte Carlo (points) vs. analytical (line) plot(   tb_grid$theta, tb_grid$rmse,   type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",   xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "RMSE", main = "RMSE: Simulation vs. Analytical",   ylim = c(0, max(c(tb_grid$rmse, mc_result$rmse)) * 1.2) ) points(mc_result$theta, mc_result$rmse, pch = 16, col = "darkorange") legend("topright",        legend = c("reval_mst() (analytical)", "run_mst() (Monte Carlo)"),        col = c("steelblue", "darkorange"), lty = c(1, NA), pch = c(NA, 16),        lwd = c(2, NA), cex = 0.8) grid() par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) sim_mc_matched <- run_mst(   x            = x,   route_map    = route_map,   module       = module,   theta        = true_theta,   D            = 1.702,   route_method = NULL,   cut_score    = cut_score,   route_score  = list(method = "INV.TCC", range.tcc = c(-5, 5)),   final_score  = list(method = "INV.TCC", range.tcc = c(-5, 5)),   se           = FALSE,   verbose      = FALSE )  # Empirical bias and RMSE at each grid point, matched-scoring condition diff_matched <- sim_mc_matched$est.theta - true_theta bias_matched <- tapply(diff_matched, true_theta, mean) rmse_matched <- tapply(diff_matched, true_theta, function(d) sqrt(mean(d^2)))  mc_result_matched <- data.frame(   theta = as.numeric(names(bias_matched)),   bias  = as.numeric(bias_matched),   rmse  = as.numeric(rmse_matched) ) mc_result_matched <- mc_result_matched[order(mc_result_matched$theta), ] compare_tb <- data.frame(   theta              = theta_grid,   analytical_bias    = round(tb_grid$bias, 3),   EAP_ML_bias        = round(mc_result$bias, 3),   INVTCC_INVTCC_bias = round(mc_result_matched$bias, 3),   analytical_rmse    = round(tb_grid$rmse, 3),   EAP_ML_rmse        = round(mc_result$rmse, 3),   INVTCC_INVTCC_rmse = round(mc_result_matched$rmse, 3) ) compare_tb[compare_tb$theta <= -3 | compare_tb$theta >= 3, ] #>    theta analytical_bias EAP_ML_bias title: Utility Functions
text: Beyond main analysis pipeline, irtQ includes set utility functions simulating item response data, computing information characteristic functions, supporting numerical integration ability scale, computing asymptotic standard errors item parameter estimates. Throughout vignette reuse two item metadata objects defined .
code: library(irtQ) set.seed(2026) # 15-item binary test (3PLM) meta_bin <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(     a = c(1.0, 1.2, 0.8, 1.4, 0.9, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.2,           0.9, 1.1, 1.4, 0.85, 1.0),     b = c(-2.0, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5, -0.1, 0.2, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.6,           -0.8, -0.3,  0.5,  1.0, 1.8),     g = rep(0.15, 15)   ),   item.id = paste0("I", 1:15),   cats    = 2,   model   = "3PLM" )  # Mixed-format test: 5 dichotomous (3PLM) + 3 polytomous (GRM, 4 categories) meta_mix <- shape_df(   par.drm = list(     a = c(1.0, 1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 0.8),     b = c(-1.0, -0.3, 0.3, 0.8, 1.4),     g = rep(0.15, 5)   ),   par.prm = list(     a = c(1.5, 1.2, 1.0),     d = list(       c(-1.5, -0.2, 1.0),       c(-1.2,  0.1, 1.3),       c(-0.9,  0.4, 1.6)     )   ),   item.id = c(paste0("DRM", 1:5), paste0("GRM", 1:3)),   cats    = c(rep(2, 5), rep(4, 3)),   model   = c(rep("3PLM", 5), rep("GRM", 3)) )  # Common theta grid used by info(), traceline(), and lwrc() theta_grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.1)

title: Utility Functions
text: simdat() generates item response matrices known IRT parameters. primary tool producing synthetic data testing demonstration. supports 1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM dichotomous items GRM GPCM polytomous items, including mixed-format tests. what: drm() and prm() — Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: drm() prm() low-level probability engines underlying simdat(), traceline(), info(), internal estimation routines. compute item response probabilities directly IRT parameters useful whenever need category probabilities specific set theta values without constructing full item metadata frame.

previous_headings: drm() and prm() — Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: drm() computes P(θ)P(\theta), probability correct response, one dichotomous items 1PLM, 2PLM, 3PLM: P(θ)=g+1−g1+exp⁡(−D⋅⋅(θ−b)), P(\theta) = g + \frac{1 - g}{1 + \exp(-D \cdot \cdot (\theta - b))},  aa discrimination, bb difficulty, gg guessing parameter (pseudo-chance level), DD scaling constant. Setting g=0g = 0 gives 2PLM; additionally fixing aa equal across items gives 1PLM. function returns matrix rows = theta values columns = items. useful check: 3PLM item, P(θ=b)=(1+g)/2P(\theta = b) = (1 + g)/2.

previous_headings: drm() and prm() — Item Response Probability Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: prm() computes category response probabilities single polytomous item GRM GPCM. returns matrix rows = theta values columns = score categories (0, 1, …, K−1K-1), rows always sum 1. d argument contains K−1K - 1 threshold parameters KK-category item: GRM: d holds K−1K - 1 difficulty thresholds bkb_k P(U≥k∣θ)=0.5P(U \geq k \mid \theta) = 0.5. categories ordered higher theta values yield higher expected scores. GPCM: d holds K−1K - 1 threshold parameters expressed item location minus step parameter category boundary. first threshold fixed 0 internally, provide K−1K - 1 values. GRM GPCM use parameter names produce different probability profiles. GRM appropriate response categories ordered increasing difficulty thresholds; GPCM allows flexible step structures. PCM (special case GPCM equal discrimination across items), set = 1.

what: info() — Item and Test Information Functions
title: Utility Functions
text: info() computes item information function (IIF) test information function (TIF) specified ability values. TIF sum IIFs reciprocal squared conditional standard error estimation: TIF(θ)=∑jIIFj(θ)=1/SE2(θ)\text{TIF}(\theta) = \sum_j \text{IIF}_j(\theta) = 1/\text{SE}^2(\theta). function returns object class "info" three components: $iif: matrix item information values (rows = items, columns = theta points), $tif: numeric vector TIF values theta point, $theta: theta grid supplied user. plot() method visualises IIFs, TIF, conditional standard error estimation (CSEE = 1/TIF1/\sqrt{\text{TIF}}).

what: traceline() — Item and Test Characteristic Curves
title: Utility Functions
text: traceline() computes item characteristic curve (ICC), test characteristic curve (TCC), category response probabilities item specified ability grid. function returns object class "traceline" four components: $prob.cats: named list data frames, one per item, containing category response probabilities (columns resp.0, resp.1, …) theta value, $icc: matrix expected item scores (rows = theta, columns = items), $tcc: numeric vector expected total (summed) scores theta, $theta: theta grid supplied user. dichotomous items, ICC equals P(θ)P(\theta), probability correct response. polytomous items, ICC expected item score ∑kk⋅P(U=k∣θ)\sum_k k \cdot P(U = k \mid \theta). plot() method used visualisation. Two key arguments control drawn: item.loc: item(s) plot; NULL plots TCC whole test. score.curve: FALSE (default) draws category response probability curves; TRUE draws expected item score curve (single curve per item). Note score.curve = FALSE overlap = FALSE, single item can specified item.loc (one panel per score category). plot multiple items simultaneously score.curve = FALSE, set overlap = TRUE (one panel per item, categories overlaid within panel).

title: Utility Functions
text: lwrc() implements Lord–Wingersky recursive algorithm (Lord Wingersky 1984; Kolen Brennan 2004), computes conditional distribution observed summed score given θ\theta: Pr⁡(X=s∣θ),s=0,1,…,∑j(Kj−1). \Pr(X = s \mid \theta), \quad s = 0, 1, \ldots, \sum_j (K_j - 1). distribution foundation IRT-based score equating used internally sx2_fit(), cac_lee(), est_score() (EAP summed-score method). tests polytomous items, algorithm generalizes straightforwardly ordered response categories. function supports two input modes: x argument (item metadata): computes conditional distribution specified theta value; returns matrix rows = summed scores (0,1,…,J0, 1, \ldots, J) columns = theta levels. prob argument (x = NULL): user provides category probability matrix already evaluated particular theta (single marginal weight), together cats vector; returns named vector summed-score probabilities. useful category probabilities come external source computing marginal distribution single fixed ability level.

previous_headings: lwrc() — Lord–Wingersky Recursion
title: Utility Functions
text: two results agree, confirming expected summed score derived lwrc() matches TCC value ability level.
code: # Conditional summed-score distribution at three ability levels lwrc_val <- lwrc(   x     = meta_bin,   theta = c(-1, 0, 1),   D     = 1.702 )  dim(lwrc_val)           # (J+1) rows × length(theta) columns: 16 × 3 #> [1] 16  3 round(head(lwrc_val), 4) #>         theta.1 theta.2 theta.3 #> score.0  0.0004  0.0000       0 #> score.1  0.0055  0.0000       0 #> score.2  0.0333  0.0001       0 #> score.3  0.1039  0.0012       0 #> score.4  0.1960  0.0087       0 #> score.5  0.2428  0.0377       0  # Verify: expected summed scores from lwrc() match the TCC from traceline() score_axis <- 0:(nrow(lwrc_val) - 1) colSums(lwrc_val * score_axis) #>   theta.1   theta.2   theta.3  #>  5.212989  8.137061 11.405212 # Cross-check with TCC from traceline() tcc_check <- traceline(x = meta_bin, theta = c(-1, 0, 1), D = 1.702)$tcc round(tcc_check, 6) #> [1]  5.212989  8.137061 11.405212

previous_headings: lwrc() — Lord–Wingersky Recursion
what: Mode 2: Using a category probability matrix (x = NULL)
title: Utility Functions
text: x = NULL, user supplies prob (rows = items, columns = score categories) cats. Importantly, columns prob matrix strictly correspond ordered score categories (.e., column 1 score 0, column 2 score 1, column 3 score 2, forth). Empty cells items fewer categories filled 0 NA. mode returns marginal score distribution single ability level probabilities computed.
code: ## Example from Kolen & Brennan (2004, p. 183): 3 dichotomous items at a fixed theta # Each row is one item; columns are P(score=0) and P(score=1) probs_3items <- matrix(   c(0.26, 0.74,   # item 1: P(0) = 0.26, P(1) = 0.74     0.27, 0.73,   # item 2     0.18, 0.82),  # item 3   nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE ) cats_3items <- c(2, 2, 2)  score_dist <- lwrc(prob = probs_3items, cats = cats_3items) score_dist       # P(X=0), P(X=1), P(X=2), P(X=3) #>  score.0  score.1  score.2  score.3  #> 0.012636 0.127692 0.416708 0.442964 sum(score_dist)  # should equal 1 #> [1] 1 ## Mixed-format: 2 dichotomous + 1 four-category + 1 three-category item p1 <- c(0.3, 0.7, NA,  NA)    # dichotomous: 2 categories (cols: 0, 1) p2 <- c(0.4, 0.6, NA,  NA)    # dichotomous: 2 categories (cols: 0, 1) p3 <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2)   # polytomous:  4 categories (cols: 0, 1, 2, 3) p4 <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2, NA)    # polytomous:  3 categories (cols: 0, 1, 2)  prob_mix <- rbind(p1, p2, p3, p4) cats_mix  <- c(2, 2, 4, 3)  score_dist_mix <- lwrc(prob = prob_mix, cats = cats_mix) score_dist_mix   # P(X=0) through P(X=7); max score = 1+1+3+2 = 7 #> score.0 score.1 score.2 score.3 score.4 score.5 score.6 score.7  #>  0.0060  0.0446  0.1410  0.2518  0.2758  0.1868  0.0772  0.0168 sum(score_dist_mix) #> [1] 1

title: Utility Functions
text: gen.weight() generates two-column data frame quadrature nodes normalised weights used numerical integration ability scale. used est_score() (EAP), sx2_fit(), cac_lee(), cac_rud(), covirt(). Three distribution options available via dist argument: "norm": normal distribution. n given (theta), Gaussian quadrature points weights computed via statmod::gauss.quad.prob(). theta given, weights proportional normal density evaluated node. "unif": uniform distribution — equally spaced nodes [l,u][l, u] equal weights. "emp": empirical distribution — equal weights user-supplied theta values. returned data frame always columns named theta weight, weights always sum 1.

what: covirt() — Asymptotic Variance-Covariance Matrices of Item Parameters
title: Utility Functions
text: covirt() computes analytical asymptotic variance-covariance matrices item parameter estimates using formulas developed Thissen Wainer (1982) extended polytomous IRT models Li Lissitz (2004). matrices provide asymptotic standard errors (ASEs) maximum likelihood estimates without requiring examinee response data — item parameters sample size used calibration needed. ASEs obtained analytically represent lower bounds true standard errors (Thissen Wainer 1982), best used approximations empirical standard errors calibration software unavailable. function returns named list two components: $cov: named list variance-covariance matrices, one per item, $se: named list ASE vectors (square roots diagonal elements covariance matrix). Notes PCM items: item metadata uses "GPCM" label Generalized Partial Credit Model (GPCM) Partial Credit Model (PCM). PCM items (discrimination fixed 1) require special handling variance computation must identified via pcm.loc argument.

what: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: goal irtQ fit unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models data may include dichotomous polytomous items. package enables: Typical item parameters estimation Pretest item calibration Multiple-group item calibration Estimation examinees’ latent abilities Evaluation model-data fit item level Item parameter estimation conducted using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). pretest item calibration, irtQ supports: Fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC; Kim, 2006), Fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC; Ban et al., 2001; Stocking, 1988). ability estimation, several widely used scoring methods available, including: Maximum likelihood estimation (ML) Maximum likelihood estimation fences (MLF; Han, 2016) Weighted likelihood estimation (WL; Warm, 1989) Maximum posteriori estimation (MAP; Hambleton et al., 1991) Expected posteriori estimation (EAP; Bock & Mislevy, 1982) EAP summed scoring (Thissen et al., 1995; Thissen & Orlando, 2001) Inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Kolen & Tong, 2010; Stocking, 1996) Also, model fit assessment includes item fit statistics : Chi-square (X²; Bock, 1960; Yen, 1981), Likelihood ratio chi-square (G²; McKinley & Mills, 1985), Infit outfit statistics (Ames et al., 2015) Graphical residual diagnostics (Hambleton et al., 1991) S-X² (Orlando & Thissen, 2000, 2003) addition, package offers variety utilities IRT analysis, including: Detecting differential item functioning (DIF) using RDIF, RDIF-CR (categorical residuals), GRDIF (multiple groups), CATSIB Detecting item parameter drift (IPD) using RIPD framework Pseudo-count D² statistic Computing classification accuracy consistency indices Designing, evaluating, simulating multistage-adaptive test (MST) panels, including TIF-crossing cut-score selection, recursion-based analytical evaluation, Monte Carlo simulation full MST administrations Simulating response data Computing conditional distribution observed scores using Lord-Wingersky recursion Calculating item test information characteristic functions Visualizing item test characteristic information curves Importing item ability parameters popular IRT software (e.g., BILOG-MG, PARSCALE, flexMIRT, mirt R package) Running flexMIRT (Cai, 2017) directly R Supporting additional tools flexible practical IRT analyses full documentation, including function references tutorial articles, visit package website: https://hwangQ.github.io/irtQ/.

what: 1. Item Calibration for a Linear Test Form
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: Item parameter estimation linear test form can performed using irtQ::est_irt() function, implements marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). function returns item parameter estimates along standard errors, computed using cross-product approximation method (Meilijson, 1989). irtQ package supports calibration mixed-format tests containing dichotomous polytomous items. also provides flexible set options address various practical calibration needs. example, users can: Specify prior distributions item parameters Fix specific parameters (e.g., guessing parameter 3PL model) Estimate latent ability distribution using nonparametric histogram method (Woods, 2007) irtQ package, item calibration linear test form typically involves two main steps: Prepare examinees’ response data set linear test form estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_irt() function, response data set linear test form must first prepared. data provided either matrix data frame format, rows represent examinees columns represent items. missing responses, properly coded (e.g., NA). Estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_irt() function estimate item parameters, several key input arguments must specified irtQ::est_irt() function: data: matrix data frame containing examinees’ item responses. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant (typically 1.702) align logistic function normal ogive model. Optionally, may incorporate prior distributions item parameters: use.aprior, use.bprior, use.gprior: Logical indicators specifying whether apply prior distributions discrimination (), difficulty (b), guessing (g) parameters, respectively. aprior, bprior, gprior: Lists specifying distributional form corresponding parameters prior. Supported distributions include Beta, Log-normal, Normal. response data contain missing values, must specify missing value code via missing argument. default, latent ability distribution assumed follow standard normal distribution (.e., N(0, 1)). However, users can estimate empirical histogram latent distribution setting EmpHist = TRUE, based nonparametric method proposed Woods (2007).

what: 2. Pretest Item Calibration with the Fixed Item Parameter Calibration (FIPC) Method (e.g., Kim, 2006)
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC) method widely used approach calibrating pretest items computerized adaptive testing (CAT). enables placement parameter estimates newly developed items onto scale operational item parameters (.e., scale item bank), without need post hoc linking rescaling procedures (Ban et al., 2001; Chen & Wang, 2016). FIPC, parameters operational items fixed, prior distribution latent ability variable estimated calibration process. estimated prior used place pretest item parameters scale fixed operational items (Kim, 2006). irtQ package, FIPC implemented following three steps: Prepare item metadata, including operational items (fixed) pretest items. perform FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function, item metadata must first prepared. item metadata structured data frame includes essential information item, number score categories IRT model type. details, refer Details section irtQ::est_irt() documentation. FIPC procedure, metadata must contain : Operational items (whose parameters fixed), Pretest items (whose parameters freely estimated). pretest items, cats (number score categories) model (IRT model type) must accurately specified. However, item parameter values (e.g., par.1, par.2, par.3) metadata serve placeholders can arbitrary, since actual parameter estimates obtained calibration. facilitate creation metadata FIPC, helper function irtQ::shape_df_fipc() can used. Prepare response data set examinees answered operational pretest items. implement FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function, examinees’ response data test form must provided, including operational pretest items. response data matrix data frame format, rows represent examinees columns represent items. Note column order response data must exactly match row order item metadata. Perform FIPC using irtQ::est_irt() function calibrate pretest items. FIPC performed using irtQ::est_irt() function, parameters pretest items estimated parameters operational items fixed. implement FIPC, must provide following arguments irtQ::est_irt(): x: item metadata, including operational pretest items. data: examinee response data corresponding item metadata. fipc = TRUE: Enables fixed item parameter calibration. fipc.method: Specifies FIPC method used (e.g., "MEM"). fix.loc: vector indicating positions operational items fixed. Optionally, may estimate empirical histogram scale latent ability distribution setting EmpHist = TRUE. EmpHist = FALSE, normal prior assumed scale updated iteratively EM algorithm. additional details implementing FIPC, refer documentation irtQ::est_irt().

what: 3. Pretest Item Calibration with the Fixed Ability Parameter Calibration (FAPC) Method (e.g., Stocking, 1988)
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: computerized adaptive testing (CAT), fixed ability parameter calibration (FAPC) method—also known Stocking’s Method (Stocking, 1988)—one simplest straightforward approaches calibrating pretest items. involves estimating item parameters using maximum likelihood estimation, conditional known estimated proficiency values. FAPC primarily used place parameter estimates pretest items onto scale operational item parameters. can also used recalibrate operational items evaluating potential item parameter drift (Chen & Wang, 2016; Stocking, 1988). method known produce accurate unbiased item parameter estimates items randomly administered examinees, rather adaptively, often case pretest items (Ban et al., 2001; Chen & Wang, 2016). irtQ package, FAPC can conducted two main steps: Prepare data set containing item response data corresponding ability (proficiency) estimates. use irtQ::est_item() function, two input data sets required: Ability estimates: numeric vector containing examinees’ ability (proficiency) estimates. Item response data: matrix data frame containing item responses, rows represent examinees columns represent items. order examinees response data must exactly match order ability estimates. Estimate item parameters using irtQ::est_item() function. irtQ::est_item() function estimates pretest item parameters based provided ability estimates. use function, must specify following arguments: data: matrix data frame containing examinees’ item responses. score: numeric vector examinees’ ability (proficiency) estimates. model: character vector specifying IRT model item (e.g., "1PLM", "2PLM", "3PLM", "GRM", "GPCM"). cats: numeric vector indicating number score categories item. dichotomous items, use 2. D: scaling constant (typically 1.702) align logistic function normal ogive model. additional details implementing FAPC, refer documentation irtQ::est_item().

what: 1. Prepare a data set for model fit analysis
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: conducting IRT model fit analysis, three key data sets must prepared: Item metadata: data frame containing item-level information, including: Item ID Number score categories IRT model specification Calibrated item parameters can either construct data frame manually generate using irtQ::shape_df() function. Additionally, item parameters estimated using IRT software (e.g., BILOG-MG 3, PARSCALE 4, flexMIRT, mirt R package), can import using corresponding irtQ::bring.*() functions (e.g., irtQ::bring.flexmirt(), irtQ::bring.bilog()). Ability estimates: numeric vector examinees’ estimated proficiency values. Response data: matrix data frame rows represent examinees columns represent items. order examinees matrix must exactly match ability estimates, column order must match item metadata.

what: 2. Compute IRT item fit statistics using irtQ::irtfit()
title: irtQ: Unidimensional Item Response Theory Modeling
text: irtQ::irtfit() function calculates widely used item fit statistics, including: Chi-square (X²) Likelihood-ratio chi-square (G²) Infit outfit statistics compute X² G² statistics, latent ability scale must divided several groups. Two grouping methods available: "equal.width": Divides scale intervals equal length "equal.freq": Divides scale groups equal numbers examinees must also specify expected probabilities item responses calculated within group. Two options available: "average": Uses average ability estimate within group "middle": Uses midpoint interval implement step, specify item metadata (x), ability estimates (score), response data (data) arguments irtQ::irtfit() function. want use fewer ten ability groups, adjust n.width argument accordingly. response data contain missing values, specify missing value code using missing argument. Upon execution, function returns item fit statistics contingency tables used compute X² G² statistics. Note model-fit evaluation using S-X² statistic can implemented using irtQ::sx2_fit() function.

Supported methods include:  "cp": Clopper–Pearson interval (Clopper & Pearson, 1934) "wilson": Wilson score interval (Wilson, 1927) "wilson.cr": Wilson score interval continuity correction (Newcombe, 1998) graphical diagnostics complement statistical fit measures, allowing deeper investigation adequacy model fit individual items.

title: Residual-Based DIF Detection Framework Using Categorical Residuals (RDIF-CR) — crdif
text: According Penfield (2010), differential item functioning (DIF) polytomously scored items can conceptualized two forms: global DIF net DIF. Global DIF refers differences groups conditional probabilities responding specific score categories, thus offering fine-grained view DIF category level. contrast, net DIF summarizes differences single value representing overall impact DIF item’s expected score. RDIF framework using categorical residuals (RDIF-CR), implemented crdif(), extends original residual-based DIF framework proposed Lim et al. (2022) detect global DIF polytomous items. framework includes three statistics: \(RDIF_{R}-CR\), \(RDIF_{S}-CR\), \(RDIF_{RS}-CR\), designed capture different aspects group-level differences categorical response patterns. illustrate RDIF-CR framework operates, consider item five ordered score categories (\(k \\{0,1,2,3,4\}\)). Suppose examinee latent ability \(\theta\) responds category 2. one-hot encoded response vector response \((0,0,1,0,0)^T\). Assume IRT model estimates examinee’s expected score 2.5 predicts category probabilities \((0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.25, 0.05)^T\). RDIF-CR framework, categorical residual vector calculated subtracting predicted probability vector one-hot response vector, resulting \((-0.1, -0.2, 0.6, -0.25, -0.05)^T\). contrast RDIF-CR framework, net DIF assessed using unidimensional item score residual. example, residual \(2 - 2.5 = -0.5\). detecting net DIF, rdif() function used instead. Note dichotomous items, crdif() rdif() yield identical results. categorical probability vector binary item reduces scalar difference, making global net DIF evaluations mathematically equivalent.

title: Item parameter estimation using MMLE-EM algorithm — est_irt
text: function fits unidimensional item response theory (IRT) models mixed-format data comprising dichotomous polytomous items, using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation–maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). also supports fixed item parameter calibration (FIPC; Kim, 2006), practical method pretest (newly developed) item calibration computerized adaptive testing (CAT). FIPC enables parameter estimates pretest items placed scale operational items (Ban et al., 2001). dichotomous items, function supports one-, two-, three-parameter logistic models. polytomous items, supports graded response model (GRM) (generalized) partial credit model (GPCM).

title: Multiple-group item calibration using MMLE-EM algorithm — est_mg
text: function performs multiple-group item calibration (Bock & Zimowski, 1997) using marginal maximum likelihood estimation via expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). also supports multiple-group fixed item parameter calibration (MG-FIPC; e.g., Kim & Kolen, 2016), extends single-group FIPC method (Kim, 2006) multiple-group settings. dichotomous items, function supports one-, two-, three-parameter logistic IRT models. polytomous items, graded response model (GRM) (generalized) partial credit model (GPCM) available.

title: Multiple-group item calibration using MMLE-EM algorithm — est_mg
text: Multiple-group (MG) item calibration (Bock & Zimowski, 1996) provides unified framework handling testing scenarios involving multiple groups, nonequivalent groups equating, vertical scaling, identification differential item functioning (DIF). applications, examinees different groups typically respond either test form different forms share common (anchor) items. goal MG item calibration estimate item parameters latent ability distributions groups simultaneously (Bock & Zimowski, 1996). irtQ package implements MG calibration via est_mg() function, uses marginal maximum likelihood estimation expectation-maximization (MMLE-EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981). addition, function supports multiple-group fixed item parameter calibration (MG-FIPC; e.g., Kim & Kolen, 2016), allows parameters specific items fixed across groups. MG IRT analyses, common multiple groups' test forms share common (anchor) items. default, est_mg() function automatically constrains items identical item IDs across groups share parameter estimates. features est_mg() function similar est_irt() function. main difference several arguments est_mg() accept list objects containing elements group analyzed. arguments include x, data, model, cats, item.id, fix.loc fix.id. Additionally, est_mg() introduces two new arguments: group.name free.group. group.name argument required assign unique identifier group. order list elements provided x, data, model, cats, item.id, fix.loc fix.id must match order group names specified group.name argument. free.group argument required indicate groups latent ability distribution scales (.e., mean standard deviation) freely estimated. item parameters fixed (.e., fipc = FALSE), least one group must fixed latent ability scale (e.g., mean = 0 variance = 1) among multiple groups sharing common items, order resolve scale indeterminacy inherent IRT estimation. specifying groups free.group argument, scales groups freely estimated, scales groups included free.group fixed using values provided group.mean group.var arguments weights argument. Situations requiring implementation MG-FIPC typically arise new latent ability scales multiple-group (MG) test data need linked established scale (e.g., existing item bank). single run MG-FIPC procedure, parameters non-fixed (freed) items across multiple test forms, well latent ability distributions multiple groups, can estimated scale fixed items (Kim & Kolen, 2016). example, suppose three different test forms—Form 1, Form 2, Form 3—administered three nonequivalent groups: Group1, Group2, Group3. Form 1 Form 2 share 12 common items (C1I1 C1I12), Form 2 Form 3 share 10 common items (C2I1 C2I10). common items Form 1 Form 3. Also, assume unique items Form 1 existing item bank already calibrated item bank's scale. case, goal MG-FIPC estimate parameters items across three test forms—except unique items Form 1— latent ability distributions three groups, scale item bank. achieve , unique items Form 1 must fixed MG-FIPC link current MG test data item bank scale. est_mg() function can implement MG-FIPC setting fipc = TRUE. case, information items fix must provided either fix.loc fix.id argument. using fix.loc, must supply list item positions (locations) fixed group’s test form. example, suppose test data three groups analyzed. first group, 1st, 3rd, 5th items fixed; second group, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 7th items fixed; third group, 1st, 2nd, 6th items fixed. case, specify: fix.loc = list(c(1, 3, 5), c(2, 3, 4, 7), c(1, 2, 6)). title: Estimate examinees' ability (proficiency) parameters — est_score
text: function estimates examinees' latent ability parameters. Available scoring methods include maximum likelihood estimation (ML), maximum likelihood estimation fences (MLF; Han, 2016), weighted likelihood estimation (WL; Warm, 1989), maximum posteriori estimation (MAP; Hambleton et al., 1991), expected posteriori estimation (EAP; Bock & Mislevy, 1982), EAP summed scoring (Thissen et al., 1995; Thissen & Orlando, 2001), inverse test characteristic curve (TCC) scoring (e.g., Kolen & Brennan, 2004; Kolen & Tong, 2010; Stocking, 1996).

title: Estimate examinees' ability (proficiency) parameters — est_score
code: est_score(x, ...)  # Default S3 method est_score(   x,   data,   D = 1,   method = "ML",   range = c(-5, 5),   norm.prior = c(0, 1),   nquad = 41,   weights = NULL,   fence.a = 3,   fence.b = NULL,   tol = 1e-04,   max.iter = 100,   se = TRUE,   stval.opt = 1,   intpol = TRUE,   range.tcc = c(-7, 7),   missing = NA,   ncore = 1,   ... )  # S3 method for class 'est_irt' est_score(   x,   method = "ML",   range = c(-5, 5),   norm.prior = c(0, 1),   nquad = 41,   weights = NULL,   fence.a = 3,   fence.b = NULL,   tol = 1e-04,   max.iter = 100,   se = TRUE,   stval.opt = 1,   intpol = TRUE,   range.tcc = c(-7, 7),   missing = NA,   ncore = 1,   ... )

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: Computes routing cut scores multistage test (MST) identifying theta values adjacent modules' Test Information Functions (TIFs) cross correct direction. resulting cut scores can passed directly run_mst cut_score argument (route_method = NULL), providing principled psychometrically grounded alternative heuristic cut-score selection.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: run_mst uses Maximum Fisher Information (MFI) routing (route_method = "mfi"), selects next-stage module maximizes TIF examinee's current ability estimate. principle, harder module always higher TIF high-ability examinees, lower TIF low-ability examinees, making MFI routing work intended. However, practice, harder module's TIF curve can peak theta value unexpectedly low, harder module also highest TIF near low end ability scale. case, low-ability examinee incorrectly routed harder module – opposite MST designed , called anomalous routing path reversal.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: find_cut() resolves problem computing cut scores TIF curves , rather relying pure MFI time routing. Specifically, pair adjacent modules (ordered mean item difficulty), function finds theta value harder module's TIF first overtakes easier module's TIF theta increases. crossing point natural boundary two modules: , easier module informative; , harder module informative. Using point fixed cut score pre-empts path reversal problem entirely.

title: Find TIF-Crossing Cut Scores for MST Routing — find_cut
text: Two TIF curves may cross . find_cut() distinguishes two types crossing: Proper crossing: difference \(\text{TIF}_{\text{harder}}(\theta) - \text{TIF}_{\text{easier}}(\theta)\) changes sign negative positive (positive slope crossing). correct, expected crossing middle theta scale. Anomalous crossing: difference changes sign positive negative (negative slope crossing). corresponds pathological situation harder module temporarily dominates low end theta scale – exactly pattern causes path reversals MFI routing. proper crossings used cut scores. Anomalous crossings reported $details diagnostic purposes excluded returned cut_score. proper crossing found module pair, informative error thrown. multiple proper crossings found (unusual well-designed modules), warning issued one closest ref_theta selected.
